title: Legend 01: Jesse Livermore
hook: Legend 01. At 14: posting stock prices, $5 a week.
takeaway: Livermore's edge was patience at a level: wait for the pivotal point, act when price crosses it, then sit tight. He made fortunes and lost them, so read the risk lessons as closely as the wins. Our Sodium tripwire is his pivotal point.
emotion: respect with a wink: awe at the patience, a wry nod to the fortunes he lost

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jesse Livermore
sources.used_for: born 1877, Shrewsbury MA; at 14 (1891) a board boy posting quotes at Paine Webber in Boston for $5 a week; stocks and commodities; big wins (1907 panic, 1929) and bankruptcy filings (1915, 1934); died 1940

sources.title: Jesse L. Livermore, How to Trade in Stocks (Duell, Sloan & Pearce, 1940), ch. V 'The Pivotal Point' (first-edition record: Bauman Rare Books)
sources.used_for: his own method, paraphrased: waiting with patience for the pivotal point before trading, then sitting tight; a stock that does not perform after crossing it is a danger signal; never average losses; no second trade if the first shows a loss

sources.title: Edwin Lefèvre, Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923), Project Gutenberg #60979
sources.used_for: the semi-fictional account of Livermore (narrator Larry Livingston): the big money came from sitting tight, not from thinking; never argue with the tape (paraphrased)

carousel.headline: Wait for the pivotal point.
carousel.sub: He traded when price reached the level that decides the move, and said patience there was what made him money.

carousel.headline: Never average a loss.
carousel.sub: His rule in How to Trade in Stocks (1940): if the first trade shows a loss, don't make a second one. He added only to a winner.

carousel.headline: Then sit tight.
carousel.sub: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator (1923): being right early is common. Sitting tight while you're right is the rare part.
